note: Dual-source extension: two candidate source domains are mapped and compared against a single target domain.

sourceDomains.name: CPU Cache (L1/L2/L3 Hardware)
sourceDomains.description: Hardware cache hierarchy sitting between CPU registers and main memory, managed automatically by the processor using LRU-family eviction and spatial-locality prefetching.

entities.name: Cache Line
entities.description: Fixed-size block (typically 64 bytes) fetched atomically; spatial locality determines efficiency

entities.name: LRU / pseudo-LRU Eviction
entities.description: Least-recently-used entry is discarded when the cache is full; implemented deterministically in hardware

entities.name: Cache Miss
entities.description: Requested data absent; processor fetches from the next slower tier (L2 → L3 → RAM)

entities.name: Hit Rate
entities.description: Fraction of accesses served from cache; high hit rate = low effective latency

entities.name: Write-back / Write-through
entities.description: Governs whether writes flush immediately to memory (write-through, always consistent) or are deferred (write-back, fast but risks stale reads on crash)

entities.name: CLFLUSH / Cache Invalidation
entities.description: Explicit instruction that evicts a specific cache line, forcing the next access to reload from memory

entities.name: Hardware Prefetcher
entities.description: Speculatively loads cache lines before they are requested, based on detected sequential or strided access patterns

entities.name: Cold Start (Post Power-On)
entities.description: Immediately after boot, the cache is fully empty; every access is a miss until the working set is loaded

relations.description: A miss under full capacity triggers eviction of the LRU line before loading the new one
Prefetcher reduces miss rate for predictable sequential access patterns

properties: Fixed total capacity at chip design time
Co-located with computation — no network hop

sourceDomains.name: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
sourceDomains.description: Globally distributed network of edge servers that cache content geographically close to end users, reducing origin load and cross-region latency.

entities.name: Edge Node / PoP
entities.description: Regional cache server close to the user; serves cached content without reaching the origin

entities.name: Origin Server
entities.description: Canonical source of truth; consulted only on cache miss or TTL expiry

entities.name: TTL / Cache-Control (max-age)
entities.description: Time-based expiry: content is considered fresh until TTL elapses, then re-validated or re-fetched from origin

entities.name: Cache Hit / Miss
entities.description: Hit: served from edge without touching origin. Miss: edge fetches from origin (or shield tier)

entities.name: Cache Purge API
entities.description: Active invalidation call that removes or refreshes content at edge nodes; propagation is asynchronous

entities.name: Eventual Consistency / Propagation Lag
entities.description: After a purge or update, edge PoPs may serve stale content for seconds-to-minutes while propagation completes

entities.name: stale-while-revalidate
entities.description: Serve stale content immediately while asynchronously refreshing from origin — keeps p99 latency flat during revalidation

entities.name: Geographic Routing (Anycast / DNS)
entities.description: Users are automatically routed to their nearest PoP via Anycast or DNS-based geolocation

relations.description: On miss, edge fetches from origin and caches the response
Purge events propagate asynchronously across PoPs, inducing a transient inconsistency window

properties: Software-managed via HTTP headers and API
TTL-driven (time-based) expiration as the primary eviction mechanism
Eventual consistency is a first-class design property, not a failure mode

targetDomain.name: Application Caching Layer (Redis / Memcached)
targetDomain.description: In-memory key-value store between application servers and the primary database; absorbs read traffic, reduces DB load, and lowers response latency. May run as a single node or a distributed cluster/replica set.

entities.name: Primary Database
entities.description: Canonical source of truth; consulted on cache miss or after TTL expiry

entities.name: Cache Entry (key-value pair)
entities.description: Atomic unit of cached data; variable size, application-defined key, optional TTL

entities.name: TTL / EXPIRE
entities.description: Time-based expiry: key is deleted when TTL elapses; next read is a miss

entities.name: LRU / allkeys-lru Eviction
entities.description: Least-recently-used key is evicted under memory pressure; Redis uses approximate (sampled) LRU, not exact

entities.name: Cache Miss Fallthrough
entities.description: Key absent from cache → application queries the database and optionally repopulates (cache-aside pattern)

entities.name: Hit Rate
entities.description: Percentage of reads served from cache without a DB query; primary performance KPI

entities.name: Explicit Invalidation (DEL / UNLINK)
entities.description: Application actively removes or overwrites a key when underlying data changes

entities.name: Cache Warming / Preloading
entities.description: Proactively populating the cache before live traffic to avoid a cold-start miss storm

entities.name: Replication / Cluster Sharding
entities.description: Redis replicas or cluster shards distribute data; introduces propagation lag between primary and replicas

relations.description: Under memory pressure, loading a new key on miss may trigger eviction of the LRU key
TTL expiry converts a previously cached key into a miss on the next access

properties: Software-managed — application code owns key lifecycle
Both TTL expiry and LRU eviction configurable simultaneously
Microsecond to low-millisecond access latency (TCP round-trip)
Single-node or distributed cluster — topology varies by deployment
No automatic coherence — application must manage consistency explicitly

mappings.justification: Structurally identical event: the fast tier fails to satisfy a request, requiring fallback to the slower authoritative store. Miss semantics, miss rate, and miss cost all transfer directly.
Both use LRU to decide which entry to discard under capacity pressure. The policy intent is identical; Redis approximates it via sampled LRU rather than exact tracking.
Hit rate is the primary performance indicator in both systems; the formula, interpretation, and optimization goal are identical.

Both are atomic units of stored data. Locality benefits transfer (related keys co-loaded = cache efficiency). However, cache lines are fixed-size (64 bytes); cache entries are variable (bytes to MB) — a meaningful asymmetry.
Write-back maps to deferred/async invalidation; write-through maps to synchronous cache update on every write. The logical tradeoff (consistency vs. write performance) is the same.
CLFLUSH (hardware cache line eviction) maps directly to DEL/UNLINK — both are active invalidation operations that force a reload on the next access.
Hardware prefetching (speculative loading based on access patterns) maps to cache warming (proactive population before live traffic). Both are strategies to avoid cold-start latency.
CPU cold start (all-empty cache post power-on) maps directly to Redis cold start after a restart or failover — the warm-up problem is structurally identical.
Origin server is the authoritative source of truth fronted by the CDN, exactly as the primary database is the authoritative source fronted by the app cache.
TTL-based expiry is structurally identical in both systems. CDN uses Cache-Control: max-age; Redis uses EXPIRE/TTL commands. The semantic model of 'freshness window' transfers completely.
Hit/miss dynamics are the same: miss → fetch from next tier → cache the response. The flow structure is isomorphic.
CDN cache purge API maps directly to Redis DEL/UNLINK — both are explicit, active invalidation operations initiated by the application when data changes.
CDN eventual consistency (propagation lag across PoPs after a purge) maps to Redis replication lag between primary and replicas after a write. Same failure mode, different scale.
stale-while-revalidate (serve stale + async refresh) maps weakly to a 'soft TTL' or 'background refresh' pattern in Redis — not native but implementable in application code.
Geographic routing (users auto-directed to nearest PoP) maps very weakly — only applies if the app cache is deployed multi-region. Single-region Redis has no routing concept.

analogyComparison.verdict: The CPU cache is the stronger primary analogy for eviction policy, hit-rate tuning, object granularity, and warm-up planning. The CDN is the stronger analogy for TTL freshness modeling, invalidation semantics, and multi-region consistency design. Neither alone is complete — use CPU cache as the default mental model and CDN when reasoning about time-based freshness or distributed propagation.

insights.description: Plan a mandatory warm-up period after every Redis restart — this is the application-layer equivalent of CPU cold-start after power-on.
insights.sourceEvidence: A CPU cache starts fully empty after boot; every access pays the full RAM latency penalty until the working set is loaded. Cache performance is noticeably degraded for a measurable warm-up period.
insights.targetApplication: Run a pre-heat script (replay a hot-key log or synthetic read workload) before routing live traffic to any restarted or newly added Redis node. Track hit rate during warm-up and gate traffic promotion on a hit-rate threshold.

insights.description: Object granularity matters as much as eviction policy: caching oversized blobs is the app-cache equivalent of cache-line false sharing.
insights.sourceEvidence: In CPU caches, false sharing occurs when unrelated data co-locates on the same 64-byte line — writes to one word invalidate the entire line for other CPUs, causing hidden coherence overhead.
insights.targetApplication: Cache data at the appropriate granularity. A 2 MB JSON blob evicted by LRU under memory pressure takes many smaller hot keys with it. Prefer caching individual objects over aggregate payloads; use separate keys for independent data.

insights.description: Model TTLs as freshness windows, not just expiry timers — the CDN Cache-Control mental model is more precise than a bare countdown.
insights.sourceEvidence: CDNs express freshness via max-age (time content is unconditionally fresh), stale-while-revalidate (serve stale; refresh async), and stale-if-error (serve stale if origin is down). Each directive answers a different operational question.
insights.targetApplication: Design Redis TTLs with three explicit questions: (1) When is data guaranteed fresh? (2) Is serving slightly stale data acceptable while refreshing? (3) What should happen if the DB is unavailable? Implement stale-while-revalidate as a 'soft TTL' background refresh pattern in your application layer.

insights.description: Treat cache invalidation across a Redis cluster as an asynchronous broadcast with a propagation window, not a synchronous guarantee.
insights.sourceEvidence: CDN purge propagation across global PoPs takes seconds to minutes by design. CDN operators accept and explicitly design for this window — they use version stamps, surrogate keys, and stale-read tolerances.
insights.targetApplication: In Redis Cluster or replica setups, write paths that DEL a key on the primary may not be visible to replica reads for up to hundreds of milliseconds. Design read paths to tolerate this window: use version stamps in cached values, or read-from-primary for consistency-critical paths.

inferences.sourcePattern: CPU caches with a working set near 100% of cache capacity experience severe thrashing — competing data continuously evicts each other, causing hit rate collapse.
inferences.targetPrediction: Redis maxmemory utilization above ~80% will show sharply elevated eviction rates and hit-rate degradation. Monitor evicted_keys/s as an early warning signal — do not wait for hit_rate to drop before scaling.

inferences.sourcePattern: Hardware prefetching is most effective for sequential, predictable access patterns. Random-access workloads defeat the prefetcher entirely.
inferences.targetPrediction: Cache warming will yield the highest ROI for predictable, repeating access patterns (e.g., daily top-N products, user dashboards). Warm-up is largely wasted effort for uniform-random or highly personalized access distributions.

inferences.sourcePattern: CDN stale-while-revalidate keeps p99 latency flat during cache revalidation storms by decoupling the response path from the refresh path.
inferences.targetPrediction: Implementing a soft-TTL pattern in Redis (return cached value + trigger async background refresh when TTL falls below a threshold) should reduce p99 latency spikes during coordinated expiry events (cache stampede). The improvement will be most pronounced when many keys share the same TTL.

limitations: CPU Cache — Fixed capacity: CPU cache size is fixed at chip design time. Redis can scale horizontally by adding nodes. Capacity planning based on the CPU cache mental model will cause you to under-estimate your scaling options and may bias you toward over-provisioning a single node.

CPU Cache — Deterministic vs. approximate eviction: CPU cache eviction is hardware-enforced and exact. Redis allkeys-lru uses sampled LRU (5 random keys, evict the worst). Do not assume precision guarantees — hot keys can and will be evicted if they're unlucky in the sample. Tune maxmemory-samples if this matters.

CPU Cache — No network hop: CPU caches are co-located with the CPU at nanosecond latency. Redis access involves a TCP round-trip (μs to low ms). The analogy breaks for latency modeling — app-cache latency is three to four orders of magnitude higher than L1 cache latency.

CPU Cache — No automatic coherence protocol: Multi-core CPUs have hardware cache coherence (MESI/MOESI). Distributed Redis instances have no automatic coherence — explicit application-level invalidation is required. Assuming 'the cache stays consistent' because the CPU cache does is a critical category error.

CPU Cache — Object size heterogeneity: Cache lines are fixed at 64 bytes; Redis values range from bytes to 512 MB. The 'unit of storage' model does not transfer for memory planning or eviction impact analysis.

CDN — Geographic distribution precondition: CDN's defining purpose is reducing cross-region latency. A single-region Redis deployment has no geographic distribution. Most of the CDN analogy's unique value (PoPs, Anycast routing, multi-region consistency) evaporates for single-region or local deployments.

CDN — Protocol mismatch: CDNs operate on HTTP with declarative Cache-Control headers; Redis is imperative — application code constructs and manages every key. The CDN mental model of 'the server declares freshness rules' does not transfer without deliberate re-implementation in application logic.

CDN — Content type assumptions: CDNs are optimized for static or semi-static, user-agnostic content (HTML, images, JS bundles). App caches frequently serve highly dynamic, user-specific data (session state, personalized feeds). The CDN staleness-tolerance assumptions do not carry over for user-specific data.

CDN — Propagation time scale: CDN purge propagation is designed to take seconds to minutes; Redis replication lag is typically sub-millisecond on healthy networks. The CDN mental model may cause you to over-engineer for propagation windows that are effectively instantaneous in your Redis topology.
